Chapter 5: Restoring the Body’s Natural Self-Regulation
Now, let’s explore the final step in this healing journey—restoring your body’s natural ability to self-regulate.
Think of it like helping your body move smoothly between moments of energy and calm, between action and rest, just the way it was meant to.
When you’ve experienced trauma, this inner flexibility often gets thrown off. Your nervous system can get stuck—either on high alert, feeling anxious or agitated, or on the other end, feeling numb and drained.
Healing is all about bringing back your body’s natural rhythm, so you can respond to life’s ups and downs, and then return to balance when things settle.
Self-regulation works a bit like your body’s own thermostat. It’s always making subtle adjustments to keep things in balance. When it’s working well, you can feel excitement, fear, sadness, and joy—all without feeling overwhelmed or completely shut down.
But after trauma, that range shrinks. Suddenly, strong emotions or sensations can feel way too much.
So, how do you start to restore that natural self-regulation? There are a few key practices that work together to support your nervous system.
First, there’s pendulation. This is simply moving your awareness back and forth—between sensations that feel uncomfortable and those that feel safe, or even just a little easier. This gentle shifting teaches your nervous system that it’s possible to feel intense things and still come back to safety.
Then we have titration. Picture breaking big, overwhelming experiences into smaller, bite-sized pieces. By working with just a little bit of sensation or emotion at a time, your body learns to process and integrate those feelings without getting flooded.
There’s also resourcing. That means finding and building up sources of comfort, strength, or safety—maybe a comforting memory, a peaceful image, or even a steady physical sensation you can come back to when things get tough.
And don’t forget grounding. This is about bringing your awareness to the present, using physical contact with the world around you—like feeling your feet on the floor, the support of your chair, or the steady rhythm of your breath. These simple anchors can help you stay connected to the here and now.
Let’s put this into a real-life example. Imagine someone who gets startled easily by sudden noises. Using pendulation, they might notice that initial jolt of fear, and then gently shift their attention to the solid feeling of their feet on the ground. By moving back and forth between those sensations, their nervous system starts to learn that it’s safe to feel activation—and that calm is always within reach.
Over time, these practices actually help widen your ability to handle all kinds of experiences. The grip of trauma starts to loosen, and many people notice they feel more resilient, adaptable, and connected—not just to themselves, but to the people around them too.
It’s important to remember, restoring self-regulation isn’t always a straight path. There will be ups and downs, and that’s okay. With patience and support, your body’s natural wisdom can start to shine through again—guiding you toward real healing and a sense of wholeness.
